summary.title: Becoming a CTO
summary.one_liner: A CTO defines long-term technology direction, communicates it in business terms, and protects the team, rather than writing the most code.
takeaways: A CTO is mainly a business strategy role that sets the long-term direction of technology, not the person who writes the most code.
The CTO must keep the technology team from becoming a pure execution arm and must have real authority over technical decisions.
Technical decisions should be weighed by business needs, customer value and return on investment, often favouring incremental updates over costly rewrites.
Reliability, security and privacy are highlighted as core priorities that business goals must respect.
The CTO should stay in sync with product managers and explain technology in plain English to non-technical people.
summary.summary: This blog post, archived on the Wayback Machine, argues that a CTO is a business strategy role rather than a senior hacker. The author describes how people often become CTOs accidentally at small companies, and says the role requires defining technology vision, protecting the team from being a pure execution arm, and holding authority over technical decisions. It covers weighing changes by ROI and the 80-20 rule, avoiding unnecessary rewrites of legacy systems, prioritising reliability, security and privacy, and communicating in plain English. The post is opinion-based and does not include code or step-by-step instructions.
